concept_html:
A pipeline is idempotent when running it twice with the same input leaves the table in the same state as running it once. Retries, reruns and redeliveries happen every week in production, so idempotence is not optional.

An append is not idempotent. Run write.mode("append") twice and every row lands twice. A Delta MERGE is idempotent when two conditions hold:

  1. The ON condition covers every column of the table's grain. For a silver table with one row per respondent per wave, that means respondent_id and wave_id.
  2. The source holds at most one row per key.

The second condition catches people out. When two source rows match the same target row, Delta cannot tell which one should win. It stops the MERGE with the error DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. When neither row matches a target row, both rows are inserted, and your grain is broken without any error.

So deduplicate the source before you merge. Rank the rows for each key by a version column, such as delivery_version or ingestion_timestamp, and keep the newest. Use a window with row_number(). Do not use dropDuplicates(): it keeps an arbitrary row per key, so a rerun keeps a different version with no warning.

The pattern for every silver load:

  • Keep the newest source row per key.
  • MERGE on the full grain.
  • whenMatchedUpdateAll() for redelivered rows, whenNotMatchedInsertAll() for new ones.

Bronze stays append-only, because bronze records every delivery as received. Silver is where you resolve versions.

exercises.solution:
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, Window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def latest_per_key(df: DataFrame, keys: list[str], order_col: str) -> DataFrame:
    """Keep the row with the highest order_col for each key.

    Args:
        df: Source rows, possibly with repeated keys.
        keys: Columns that identify one target row.
        order_col: Column that ranks versions. Highest wins.

    Returns:
        One row per key.
    """
    window = Window.partitionBy(*keys).orderBy(F.col(order_col).desc())
    return (
        df.withColumn("_rank", F.row_number().over(window))
        .filter(F.col("_rank") == 1)
        .drop("_rank")
    )

title: Idempotent MERGE, and why you deduplicate the source first
why_html:
A supplier redelivers a wave with corrected weights. The file repeats 37 respondents, because the supplier's export joined two tables. The silver job uses the reference upsert_silver, which merges without deduplicating. The MERGE fails at 02:00 with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. Gold does not refresh, and the morning Power BI report shows last week's numbers.

The on-call engineer "fixes" it by switching the job to append. The next run succeeds. Silver now holds the wave twice. Reach percentages look normal, because both the numerator and the denominator doubled. Weighted population estimates are twice their true size for a month, until a reconciliation check against the weight total catches it.

Deduplicating on the full grain before the MERGE prevents both failures.
